lead: Paul prays that the eyes of the heart may be opened to see God's power at work in the risen Christ and in his Church. Mark's short parable shows the same power working in silence: the seed grows by itself, night and day, while the farmer sleeps. The Church grows by God's power, not by our anxiety.

r.h: The eyes of your heart enlightened
set: After the great blessing of 1:3–14, Paul gives thanks and prays for his readers. In Greek the prayer runs on as one long sentence. It moves from the readers' faith and love, to hope, inheritance and power, and ends with Christ raised, seated in heaven and given as head to the Church.
str: vv. 15–16: thanksgiving for their faith and love.
vv. 17–19: the prayer: a spirit of wisdom and revelation, and the eyes of the heart enlightened to know hope, inheritance and power.
vv. 20–23: that power shown in Christ: raised, seated above every power, head over all things for the Church, his body.
kw: In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person: thought, will and love. Faith gives the heart eyes.
The Church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all”: she is filled by Christ, and his fullness dwells in her for the world.
vv: so that, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you,
And he has put all things under his feet and has made him the head over all things for the church,
An echo of Psalm 8:6. The risen Christ is Lord of all creation, and he exercises his lordship for the good of the Church.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the head of the Body, and that the Church lives from him, in him and for him (CCC 792–795, in substance). The early Church called baptism itself “enlightenment”, because it opens the eyes of the heart (CCC 1216).

set: This short parable is found only in Mark. It stands in the chapter of parables by the sea (Mark 4), after the sower and the lamp and before the mustard seed. Jesus' ministry looked small and met opposition; the parable says that God's Kingdom is already growing, though no one sees how.
str: v. 27: he sleeps and rises; the seed grows, he does not know how.
v. 28: the earth produces of itself: stalk, head, full grain.
v. 29: when the grain is ripe, the sickle and the harvest.
kw: The source of our word “automatic”. The growth comes from the seed and the soil, that is, from God, not from the farmer's effort.
The harvest image comes from Joel 3:13: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.” Harvest is a biblical picture of the end of the age.
vv: and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
The farmer is not lazy; he has sown. But he cannot make the seed grow. This frees us from the anxiety of thinking that everything depends on us.
The earth produces of itself, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head.
Growth has stages. Patience belongs to faith.
ch: The Second Vatican Council compares the Kingdom to a seed: the word of the Lord, sown in the field, grows by its own power until the harvest (Lumen Gentium 5, in substance). The Church sows and trusts; the growth is God's.

study: What would I see differently if the “eyes of my heart” were enlightened?
Where must I sow and then trust, instead of trying to force the growth?
